title: Properties of materials: which let light through, and which keep water out

summary.text: You can see clearly through a clear polythene bag. So does water go through it too? Your child tests five materials from home. They look at a window through each one, and pour a spoon of water on each one. Light passes through the polythene, but the water stays on top. Your child also learns words for what materials are like: waterproof, stretchy, strong, transparent, translucent and opaque.
summary.art: A glass tumbler covered with a square of clear polythene held by a rubber band, a small pool of water sitting on top, and a window with trees seen clearly through the plastic.

intro.hook: Hold a clear polythene bag up to the window. You can see the trees and the sky through it. Now guess: if you pour water on it, will the water go through too?
intro.text: Most children guess yes. If light can get through, water should get through too. You are going to test it. A property is what a material is like, such as waterproof or see-through. Every material has many properties. Some of them surprise us, so we test them.
intro.art: A child holding a clear polythene bag up to a window, with a thinking bubble showing a drop of water.

outcomes: By the end I can describe a material with the words waterproof, stretchy, strong, transparent, translucent and opaque.
By the end I can test which materials let light through and which let water through.
By the end I can explain why clear polythene lets light through but keeps water out, and why a tea strainer lets both through.
By the end I can say that one material has many properties, and that the job decides which ones matter.
By the end I can show that strong and stretchy are two different properties, and that a thread is strong for pulling but not for pushing.
By the end I can guess first, give a reason, and then say what my test showed.

terms.meaning: What a material is like. Hard, soft, waterproof and see-through are properties.
terms.example: Two properties of a steel plate: it is hard, and it keeps water out.
terms.art: A steel plate with three small labels around it: hard, shiny, waterproof.

terms.example: An umbrella, a polythene bag and a steel tumbler are waterproof.
terms.art: Rain running off an open black umbrella.

terms.meaning: Lets light through so well that you can see clearly through it.
terms.example: Window glass, spectacles and a clear polythene bag are transparent.
terms.art: A face seen clearly through a glass window.

terms.meaning: Lets some light through, but you cannot see a clear picture through it.
terms.example: A thin cotton hanky held up to a window glows, but you cannot see the trees.
terms.art: A white cotton hanky held up to a bright window, glowing, with only a blur behind it.

terms.meaning: Does not let light through. You cannot see through it at all.
terms.example: Kitchen foil, a steel plate and a wooden door are opaque.
terms.art: A torch shining on a sheet of foil, with no light coming out the other side.

terms.meaning: Gets longer when you pull it, without breaking.
terms.example: A rubber band and a hair band are stretchy. A cotton thread hardly stretches.
terms.art: Two fingers pulling a rubber band long.

terms.example: A cotton rope is strong. A paper napkin is not.
terms.art: A cotton rope holding up a bucket of water.

terms.meaning: A very thin thread. Paper and cloth are made of fibres, with tiny gaps between them.
terms.example: Tear a newspaper slowly and look at the edge. The fuzz you see is fibres.
terms.art: The torn edge of a newspaper, close up, with tiny hair-like fibres sticking out.

explanations.context: This card explains what a property is, and why every material has many of them.
explanations.definition: A property is what a material is like, or what it does. Every material has many properties at the same time.
explanations.description: A steel tumbler is hard, shiny, waterproof and opaque. A polythene bag is soft, waterproof, a little stretchy and transparent. No two materials have exactly the same set of properties. When we choose a material for a job, we look for the properties that job needs.
examples: A raincoat needs to be waterproof and bend when you move.
A window needs to be transparent and waterproof.
A hair band needs to be stretchy and to spring back.
explanations.art: A steel tumbler, a polythene bag and a rubber band, each with a small list of property words beside it.

explanations.concept: Why some materials keep water out
explanations.context: This card explains why water goes through a hanky but not through polythene.
explanations.definition: Water gets through a material only where there is a gap or a hole. A waterproof material has no gaps that water can pass through.
explanations.description: Cloth and paper are made of fibres, with tiny gaps between them. Water creeps into the gaps and comes out the other side. A tea strainer has holes you can see, so water runs straight through. Polythene, foil and steel have no gaps, so water stays on top. A banana leaf and a chembu leaf keep water out with a smooth, waxy skin.
examples: Water dripped through the cotton hanky in our test.
Water sat on the polythene for a whole minute.
Rasam stays on a banana leaf at a meal.
explanations.art: A close-up drawing: water drops slipping through the gaps between cloth threads, and a drop sitting on a smooth sheet of polythene.

explanations.context: This card explains three words for how much light gets through a material.
explanations.definition: Transparent materials let light through so you see a clear picture. Translucent materials let some light through, but no clear picture. Opaque materials let no light through.
explanations.description: Look through clear polythene and you see the window clearly. It is transparent. A cotton hanky glows, but the trees are gone. It is translucent. Kitchen foil looks dark. It is opaque. Even clear water is not perfectly transparent. In deep sea water, the light that comes back to your eye is blue. In 1921 the Indian scientist C. V. Raman sailed home from England and studied this blue. He showed that the water itself changes the light, and that the blue is not just the sky reflected.
examples: Transparent: a glass tumbler, spectacles, clear polythene.
Translucent: a thin hanky, a paper kite held up to the sky, your closed eyelids.
Opaque: foil, a steel plate, a wooden door.
explanations.art: Three panels: a window seen clearly through polythene, a glowing blur through a hanky, and darkness behind foil.

explanations.concept: How light gets through solid plastic
explanations.context: This card answers the puzzle from our test: how did light get through polythene that had no holes?
explanations.definition: Light is not a material, and it does not need a hole. It can travel through some solid materials, such as glass, clear plastic and water.
explanations.description: Water is a material. It is made of tiny particles, and it can only pass where there is a gap. Light is different. It can pass straight through the particles of glass and clear plastic. A tea strainer lets light through in another way, through its holes. So a material can let light through and still keep water out.
examples: A glass window lets in sunlight but keeps out rain.
A clear plastic bottle lets you see the water inside, and the water stays in.
A tea strainer lets light and water through its holes.
explanations.art: Two side-by-side drawings: water stopped on top of a sheet of plastic while light rays pass through it, and water and light both passing through the holes of a steel tea strainer.

explanations.concept: Strong and stretchy are different properties
explanations.context: This card explains that strong and stretchy are two different things, and that strong depends on how you use a material.
explanations.definition: Stretchy means a material gets longer when pulled. Strong means it is hard to break. A material can be one, both or neither.
explanations.description: A rubber band is stretchy, and it snaps if you pull too hard. A cotton thread hardly stretches, yet it can pull a toy car. Spider silk is both strong and stretchy. Kevlar, a fibre made by the scientist Stephanie Kwolek, is very strong and hardly stretches. Strong also depends on the way you use a material. A thread is strong when you pull it, but it folds up when you push it.
examples: A rubber band holds a bundle of pencils tight because it is stretchy.
A cotton thread pulls a toy car, but cannot push it.
Kite string is strong but hardly stretches.
explanations.art: A child pulling a toy car on a thread across the floor, and the same thread crumpled up when pushed.

agreed.text: Every material has many properties at the same time.
agreed.evidence: In our yes-or-no grid, the steel tumbler, polythene bag, rubber band and hanky each had a different set of answers.

agreed.text: Water gets through a material only through gaps or holes.
agreed.evidence: Under a magnifying glass, cloth and paper show tiny gaps between their fibres. Water goes through them, but not through polythene or foil, which have no gaps.

agreed.text: Light can pass through some solid materials that have no holes, such as glass and clear plastic.
agreed.evidence: A glass window lets in daylight but keeps out rain. In our test, water sat on the polythene, yet we could see the window through it.

challenging.claim: If you can see through something, water can get through it too.
challenging.for: A tea strainer and a mosquito net are see-through, and water goes straight through them.
challenging.against: A strainer and a net are see-through because of their holes. Glass and clear polythene have no holes. Light passes through them, but water stays out.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess many children make before the light and water test.

challenging.for: A rubber band snaps if you pull it too far, and a balloon pops.
challenging.against: Spider silk is very stretchy and also very strong for how thin it is. A stretchy material can still be hard to break.
challenging.context: This card is about whether stretchy and strong can go together.

challenging.claim: Glass is a very slow liquid. Old windows are thicker at the bottom because the glass has flowed down.
challenging.for: Some very old windows really are thicker at the bottom.
challenging.against: Old window glass was made by hand and came out uneven. Workers often put the thick edge at the bottom. Scientists have worked out that glass at room temperature would take far longer than the age of the Universe to flow that much.
challenging.context: This card is about a popular story about glass.

big_questions.q: Light went through the polythene, but water did not. What is different about light and water?
big_questions.hint: Water needs a gap to squeeze through. Does light need a gap?

big_questions.q: Why does a tea strainer let tea through but keep the tea leaves back?
big_questions.hint: Think about the size of the holes, and the size of the leaves.

big_questions.q: Is there anything that nothing at all can get through?
big_questions.hint: Tiny particles called neutrinos come from the Sun. Almost all of them pass right through the whole Earth.

big_questions.q: When your eyes are shut in a bright room, it is not fully dark. Are you still seeing something?
big_questions.hint: Your eyelids are translucent. What gets through them?

big_questions.q: A window keeps the rain out and lets the sky in. Is the window part of the inside of your home, or the outside?
big_questions.hint: What does it let in, and what does it keep out?

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1960s, Stephanie Kwolek was a chemist at DuPont, a company in the USA. Her team wanted a new fibre that was light and very strong, for car tyres. To make a fibre, chemists first make a liquid that is usually thick and clear, a bit like honey. A machine pushes the liquid through tiny holes, and it sets into threads. In 1965, Kwolek made a liquid that was thin and cloudy. Most chemists then thought a liquid like that was no good for making threads, and threw it away. Charles Smullen, who ran the spinning machine, did not want to try it. He worried it would block the tiny holes. Kwolek kept asking, and at last he agreed. The thread was amazingly strong and stiff. Weight for weight, the fibre that came from her work is about five times stronger than steel. It was named Kevlar. Today it is used in ropes, gloves and helmets that protect people. The cloudy liquid looked useless. Only a test showed how strong its threads could be.
how_we_found_out.who: Stephanie Kwolek, an American chemist at DuPont, and Charles Smullen, who ran the spinning machine
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a liquid for making fibres had to be thick and clear, so a thin, cloudy one was useless. Kwolek had her cloudy liquid spun, and it made one of the strongest fibres ever.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman chemist in a 1960s laboratory holding up a glass jar of cloudy liquid, with a spool of shiny golden fibre on the bench beside her.

story.title: The Window That Let the Sky In
story.note: Kochi gets heavy monsoon rain from about June to September. Thangam, Vinu, Amma, Ammamma and Reshma are made up.
text: Thangam was seven. She lived with her mother, her grandmother and her little brother Vinu, on the fourth floor of a block of flats in Kochi, in Kerala.
In the monsoon, the rain in Kochi does not just fall. It pours for hours, and the wind blows it sideways.
One wet afternoon, Vinu was bouncing a ball in the kitchen. He was five. The ball flew up and hit the kitchen window. Crack! A long line ran across the glass.

Ammamma, their grandmother, came at once. "Stand back, both of you," she said. She put on thick gloves. Carefully, she lifted the cracked glass out of the frame and wrapped it in old newspaper. "Broken glass is sharp," she said. "Only a grown-up touches it."
Now there was a hole where the glass had been. Rain blew straight in, onto the shelf of steel tins.
"The glass shop is shut until tomorrow," said Amma, their mother. "We need something to cover the hole tonight."
Vinu ran to fetch a big piece of cardboard from an old box. Amma taped it over the hole. The rain stopped coming in. But the kitchen went dark.
"I can't see the rice in the pot," said Ammamma. "And my curry leaf plant by the window needs the daylight."

So they took the cardboard down. Thangam fetched a thin cotton towel, and Amma pinned it over the hole. Now the kitchen was bright again, with a soft white glow. But soon the towel was dark with water. Drops fell from the bottom of it onto the floor.
"The cardboard keeps the rain out, but it keeps the light out too," said Thangam. "The towel lets the light in, but it lets the rain in too."
"What about the tea strainer?" said Vinu. "You can see through it."
Everybody laughed, even Vinu. A tea strainer is full of tiny holes. The rain would pour through it, just like tea.
Thangam sat on the kitchen step and thought. "We need something we can see through, that has no holes at all."
Then she remembered. When Amma bought new pillows, they had come in a big, clear plastic bag. It was folded on top of the cupboard.

Thangam climbed on a stool and brought it down. She held it up to the hole. Through the plastic she could see the coconut trees, the grey sky and the rain. "Look!" she said. "It is like glass, but it is soft."

Amma taped the plastic over the hole and pulled it tight. They waited. Rain hit the plastic and ran down the outside in little streams. Not one drop came in. And the kitchen was full of grey daylight.
Vinu frowned. "But how does the light get in, if there is no hole?"
"Light doesn't need a hole," said Thangam. "It goes through the plastic itself. Rain is water, and water needs a gap to get through. This plastic has no gaps."
Vinu pressed his nose to the plastic. It was cold, and it smelled of new pillows. Outside, a crow sat on a wire, shaking the rain from their feathers. Vinu could see every drop.
Next morning, Reshma came from the glass shop with a new pane of glass. She fitted it into the frame and pressed soft putty along the edges.
"Glass does two jobs at once," Reshma told Vinu. "It lets the light in and keeps the rain out. It is also stiff and strong, so the wind cannot push it in."
Thangam folded the plastic bag and put it back on top of the cupboard.
"Keep it safe," said Ammamma. "One day we may need a window again."
story.epiphany: A window needs two properties at the same time: it must let light through and keep water out. Glass and clear plastic do both, because they have no holes, yet light passes through them.
ask: Why did the cardboard not work as a window?
Why did everyone laugh when Vinu said 'tea strainer'?
How did Thangam explain that light got in with no hole?
art: A kitchen in a Kochi flat in heavy monsoon rain, with a grandmother in thick gloves lifting a cracked pane of glass out of the window frame while a girl and a small boy watch from the doorway.
A girl holding a clear plastic bag up to an empty window frame, with coconut trees and grey rain seen clearly through it, and a small boy looking up at her.

experiments.title: Light and Water: what gets through?
experiments.context: In this experiment you look at a window through five materials. Then you put each one over a glass tumbler and pour a teaspoon of water on it. You find out which materials let light through, which let water through, and whether they are the same ones.
experiments.question: Which materials let light through, and which let water through? If light gets through a material, does water always get through too?
experiments.predict: Look at the five materials. For each one, guess: will light get through? Will water get through? Most of all, guess about the clear polythene. You can see through it. So will water go through it too? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every material gets the same two tests. For the light test, we hold each one close to one eye and look at the same window. For the water test, each one covers the same tumbler and gets 1 teaspoon of water. We wait 1 minute every time before we look.
results_table: Light: a clear picture, only a glow, or dark?
Water: stayed on top, or got through?

materials.item: a square of clear polythene, about 12 cm by 12 cm, cut from a clean, clear food bag or carry bag
a square of kitchen foil, about 12 cm by 12 cm, with no holes (or the shiny inside of an empty snack packet, washed and dried)
a square of old thin cotton cloth, such as a hanky, a dupatta or an old shirt
a square of newspaper, about 12 cm by 12 cm
a steel tea strainer
a glass tumbler (a clear plastic cup works too, or a steel tumbler if you look inside)
a rubber band that fits round the top of the tumbler
a teaspoon and a cup of water
a tray or a steel plate, and a dry cloth to wipe the tumbler
a window with daylight, or a lit tube light

experiments.safety: Look at a window or a tube light, never straight at the Sun. Looking at the Sun can hurt your eyes, even through a material.

schedule.what: Guess for each material. Look at the window through each one. Pour a teaspoon of water on each one over the tumbler. Fill in the table and say what you found.

experiments.record: Write your guesses at the top, with your reason for the polythene. Fill in the table. Draw the polythene and the tea strainer with water on them.

setup.art: Five materials laid out on a tray: a square of clear polythene, a square of foil, a square of cotton cloth, a square of newspaper and a steel tea strainer.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the five materials.

setup.art: A child holding a square of clear polythene close to one eye, looking at a window with trees outside.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the window through each one.

setup.art: A glass tumbler on a tray with polythene stretched over the top and held by a rubber band, and a child pouring a teaspoon of water onto it.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the tumbler. Pour one teaspoon of water.

setup.art: Two tumblers side by side: one with water sitting on polythene and a dry tumbler below, one with a tea strainer on top and water at the bottom of the tumbler.
setup.caption: 4. Wait one minute. Did the water get into the tumbler?

flow.do: 1. Lay out the five materials on the tray. 2. Let your child touch each one. 3. Ask the questions below. 4. Write their guesses and their reason for the polythene.
flow.say: We will do two tests on each one. Will light get through? Will water get through? Guess for each one. Now look at the polythene. You can see through it. Will water go through it too? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Touch each material. Guess: will light get through? Will water get through? Say why for the polythene.

ask.q: Will water go through the polythene? Why?
good: Yes, because I can see through it, so it must be open.
No, because a polythene bag holds water.
Yes, because it is thin.

flow.parent: Don't say if a guess is right. Many children say yes, because they can see through it. Any guess with a reason is good.
flow.context: This is the first step of the light and water test. You guess what each material will let through.

flow.do: 1. Stand by the window together. 2. Your child holds each material about 2 cm from one eye. 3. They look at the window through it. 4. They say: a clear picture, only a glow, or dark. 5. Write it in the table.
flow.say: Hold it close to one eye and look at the window. Can you see the trees clearly? Is there only a glow? Or is it dark?
flow.kid: Hold it near one eye. Look at the window. Clear picture, a glow, or dark?

ask.q: Which ones gave a clear picture?
good: The polythene, because I could see the trees.
The tea strainer, through the little holes.

flow.parent: The polythene gives a clear picture. The strainer gives a picture through its holes, a little dim. The cloth glows. The newspaper glows faintly, with print in the way. The foil is dark. Remind your child never to look at the Sun.

check.q: The foil let no light through. Which word is right for the foil?
check.why: Opaque means no light gets through. Transparent means you see a clear picture. Translucent means only a glow.

flow.context: In this step of the light and water test, you look at a window through each material.

flow.do: 1. Stand the glass tumbler on the tray. 2. Lay the polythene over the top. 3. Hold it on with the rubber band. 4. Press the middle gently so it dips a little, like a bowl.
flow.say: We put the polythene over the tumbler like a lid. If water gets through, we will see it at the bottom of the tumbler.
flow.kid: Put the polythene on the tumbler. Hold it on with the rubber band. Make a little dip in the middle.
flow.parent: The dip stops the water rolling off the edge. Keep the polythene fairly tight, so it does not touch the bottom.
flow.context: In this step of the light and water test, you cover the tumbler with the first material.

flow.do: 1. Pour 1 teaspoon of water slowly into the middle. 2. Count slowly to 60. 3. Look at the tumbler from the side. 4. Lift the cover and feel the bottom of it. 5. Write the result. 6. Wipe the tumbler dry and do the next one. 7. Rest the strainer on top instead of using the band.
flow.say: Pour the water slowly into the middle. Now count to sixty with me. Look at the bottom of the tumbler. Is there any water? Feel underneath the cover. Is it wet or dry?
flow.kid: Pour one spoon of water in the middle. Count to sixty. Look in the tumbler. Is there water? Feel under the cover.

ask.q: Which ones kept the water out?
good: The polythene and the foil. The water sat on top.
The tumbler stayed dry under them.

flow.parent: Water sits on the polythene and the foil, and the tumbler stays dry. It drips through the cloth within a few seconds. The newspaper soaks it up and goes soggy. It is wet underneath, and a few drops may fall. Count that as 'got through'. Water runs straight through the strainer.
flow.context: In this step of the light and water test, you pour water on each material and see if it gets into the tumbler.

flow.do: 1. Put the polythene and the strainer side by side. 2. Ask your child to look closely at each, and hold each up to the window. 3. Ask the questions below. 4. Listen to their answer before you explain.
flow.say: You could see through the polythene and through the strainer. But water went through only one of them. Look closely. What does the strainer have that the polythene does not? Then how did the light get through the polythene?
flow.kid: Look closely at the strainer and the polythene. What does the strainer have? How did light get through the polythene?

ask.q: Why did water go through the strainer but not the polythene?
good: The strainer has holes. The polythene has none.
Water needs a gap. Light went through the plastic itself.

flow.parent: After your child answers, say it plainly. The strainer is see-through because of its holes, so water gets through. The polythene has no holes, so water stays on top. Light passes through the plastic itself.
flow.think: Can you think of something else that lets light in but keeps water out?
flow.context: This is the last step of the light and water test. You compare the polythene and the tea strainer.

activities.title: One Thing, Many Properties: the yes-or-no grid
activities.context: In this activity you ask four questions about four things from home. You find that every thing has many properties, and no two things give the same answers.

materials.item: a steel tumbler, a polythene bag, a rubber band and a cotton hanky
a sheet of paper with a grid: four rows (one for each thing) and four columns (see-through, waterproof, stretchy, strong)
a pencil

schedule.what: Ask four questions about each of four things. Mark yes, no or a bit. Compare the rows.

activities.record: The filled-in grid, with a tick for yes, a cross for no, and a small dot for 'a bit'.

setup.art: A steel tumbler, a polythene bag, a rubber band and a cotton hanky on a table beside a paper grid with four rows and four columns.
setup.caption: 1. Put the four things beside the grid.

setup.art: A child gently pulling a polythene bag with both hands, and the grid with ticks and crosses in the first rows.
setup.caption: 2. Ask the four questions about each thing. Mark the grid.

flow.do: 1. Draw the grid with your child. 2. Write the four things down the side. 3. Write four words across the top: see-through, waterproof, stretchy, strong.
flow.say: We will ask four questions about each thing. Can I see through it? Does it keep water out? Does it stretch? Is it hard to break?
flow.kid: Help draw the grid. Write the four things down the side. Write the four words across the top.

flow.do: 1. For each thing, your child looks through it, pulls it gently, and squeezes or tugs it. 2. For waterproof, they think about whether water would go through. 3. Mark a tick, a cross or a dot for 'a bit'.
flow.say: Look through the tumbler. Can you see through it? Now pull the rubber band. Does it stretch? Try to tear the hanky gently. Is it hard to break?
flow.kid: Look through it. Pull it gently. Try to tear it gently. Mark the grid.
flow.parent: Rough answers are fine. Tumbler: not see-through, waterproof, not stretchy, strong. Polythene: see-through, waterproof, a bit stretchy, a bit strong. Rubber band: not see-through, waterproof, stretchy, a bit strong. Hanky: only a glow, not waterproof, a bit stretchy, strong.

flow.do: 1. Look at the four rows together. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the rows. Do any two things have exactly the same answers?
flow.kid: Look at the rows. Are any two the same?

ask.q: Are any two rows the same?
good: No. Every thing has its own mix.
The tumbler and the band are both waterproof, but only the band stretches.

flow.parent: Every row is different. Each material has many properties, and its own mix of them.

activities.title: Pull, Not Push: which way is a thread strong?
activities.context: In this activity you tie a cotton thread to a small toy. You try to pull the toy with the thread, then push it. Then you try the same with a pencil.

materials.item: a piece of cotton thread or string, about 50 cm long
a small toy car, an empty matchbox or a steel katori
sticky tape
a pencil

schedule.what: Pull the toy with a thread, then try to push it. Do the same with a pencil. Say which is strong in which way.

activities.record: Draw the thread pulling the toy, and the thread trying to push it. Write 'pull: yes or no' and 'push: yes or no' under each.

setup.art: A child pulling a toy car across a floor with a cotton thread taped to its front.
setup.caption: 1. Tape the thread to the toy. Pull it along.

setup.art: A child pushing the end of a thread towards a toy car, with the thread crumpling into loops.
setup.caption: 2. Now try to push the toy with the thread.

setup.art: A child pushing the same toy car with the tip of a pencil.
setup.caption: 3. Try pulling and pushing with a pencil.

flow.do: 1. Tape one end of the thread to the front of the toy. 2. Your child pulls the toy across the floor with the thread.
flow.say: Pull the toy along with the thread. Is the thread strong enough?
flow.kid: Pull the toy with the thread. Does it come?

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess if the thread can push the toy, and why. 2. Let them try to push the toy away using only the thread.
flow.say: The thread pulled the toy easily. Can it push the toy too? Why do you think so? Now try it.
flow.kid: Can the thread push the toy? Guess and say why. Now try.

good: The thread went floppy and bent.
The toy did not move.

flow.do: 1. Now your child pulls and pushes the toy with the pencil. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: The pencil can push and pull. The thread can only pull. So is the thread strong or weak?
flow.kid: Push the toy with the pencil. Pull it too. Is the thread strong or weak?

good: It is strong when you pull it.
It is no good for pushing, because it bends.

flow.parent: A thread is strong when pulled, and floppy when pushed. That is why ropes, kite strings and cables pull things, and posts and pillars push.

check.q: Which job suits a rope best?
options: Holding up a roof from below, like a pillar
Pulling a bucket up from a well
check.why: A rope is strong when pulled, so it can lift a bucket. Pushed, it bends, so it cannot hold up a roof from below or push a car.

activities.title: The Tight Bundle: why a hair band holds
activities.context: In this activity you hold one bundle of pencils with a rubber band and one with a cotton thread. Then you take some pencils out of each bundle and see which one still holds tight.

materials.item: 20 pencils, crayons or sketch pens (two bundles of 10)
a rubber band
a piece of cotton thread, about 40 cm long

schedule.what: Make two bundles. Take 3 pencils out of each. Hold them up and see which bundle stays tight.

activities.record: Draw both bundles after 3 pencils came out. Write which one stayed tight.

setup.art: Two bundles of ten pencils on a table, one wrapped twice with a rubber band, one tied with a cotton thread.
setup.caption: 1. Make two bundles of 10: one with a rubber band, one with a thread.

setup.art: A child pulling three pencils out of the middle of each bundle.
setup.caption: 2. Pull 3 pencils out of each bundle.

setup.art: The rubber band bundle held up tight, and the thread bundle with pencils sliding out onto the table.
setup.caption: 3. Hold each bundle up by the top.

flow.do: 1. Make a bundle of 10 pencils with the rubber band, wrapped twice. 2. Make a bundle of 10 with the thread. 3. Wrap the thread twice, pull it tight and tie a knot.
flow.say: Both bundles are tight now. Feel them.
flow.kid: Make two bundles. One with a rubber band. One with a thread. Feel them.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess what will happen when 3 pencils come out of each, and why. 2. Help them pull 3 pencils out of the middle of each bundle. 3. Hold each bundle up by the top.
flow.say: We will take 3 pencils out of each. Which bundle will stay tight? Why do you think so? Now let's try.
flow.kid: Guess which bundle stays tight. Say why. Pull out 3 pencils from each. Hold them up.

good: The rubber band bundle stayed tight.
The thread went loose, and pencils slid out.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below. 2. Point at the band, which is now shorter.
flow.say: Why did the rubber band still hold the pencils?
flow.kid: Why did the rubber band still hold? Look at it.

ask.q: Why did the rubber band keep holding?
good: It was stretched, and it got shorter to hold the pencils that were left.
The thread cannot get shorter, so it went loose.

flow.parent: The rubber band was stretched round the bundle. When pencils came out, it shrank back and stayed tight. A thread hardly stretches, so it stays the same length and goes loose. This is why hair bands, waistbands and fruit sellers' bands are stretchy.

games.title: Four Boxes
games.context: This is a sorting game. Each card shows a thing from home. You put it in one of four boxes: see-through or not, and keeps water out or lets it through.

printables.title: The four-box board, drawn on a big sheet of paper
items: Box 3: Not see-through, keeps water out
Box 4: Not see-through, lets water through

items.b: See-through, lets water through. Its holes let both through.
See-through, lets water through. Its holes let both through.
See-through, lets water through. Its holes let both through.
See-through, lets water through. Its holes let both through.
Not see-through, lets water through, very slowly. That is how a matka keeps water cool.

rules: Draw the board: a big square split into four boxes, with the labels written in.
Shuffle the 16 cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Turn over the top card, read it, and put it in a box. Say why.
Then turn the card over and read the back. If you were right, keep the card in the box. If not, move it, and say why it goes there.
Each right card scores one point. When all 16 are placed, the player with the most points wins. Playing alone, try to beat your own score next time.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper split into four boxes with labels, and a pile of small cards beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the four-box board. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: A child placing a card that says 'A steel tea strainer' into the box 'See-through, lets water through'.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over a card. Put it in a box. Say why.

flow.do: 1. Draw the board with your child. 2. Cut out the cards. 3. Read the four box labels together.
flow.say: Every thing goes in one box. See-through means you can see a clear picture through it.
flow.kid: Draw the four boxes. Read the labels. Cut out the cards.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over a card. 2. The player puts it in a box and says why. 3. Read the back and score.
flow.say: A mosquito net. Can you see through it? Does water go through it? Which box? Why?
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Can you see through it? Does water go through? Pick a box.

ask.q: Why did you put the mosquito net in box 2?
good: I can see through it, and water goes through the holes.

flow.parent: Box 2 is the one that surprises most children. Everything in it is see-through because of holes. Box 1 things are see-through with no holes.

flow.do: 1. Look at boxes 1 and 2 together. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Everything in boxes 1 and 2 is see-through. What is different about the things in box 2?
flow.kid: Look at box 1 and box 2. What do box 2 things have?

ask.q: What do all the box 2 things have?
good: Holes.
Little gaps that water can get through.

games.title: Go Through or Freeze!
games.players: 2 or more players, with one caller
games.context: This is a running and jumping game. The caller reads a card, such as 'Light meets foil'. If it would go through, the players jump forward. If it would be stopped, they freeze.

items.b: Goes through the holes. Jump forward.
Goes through the holes. Jump forward.
Goes through the gaps. Jump forward.
Soaks in and gets through. Jump forward.
Goes through the holes. Jump forward.

items.f: A mosquito meets a mosquito net
items.b: Stopped. The holes are too small. Freeze.
A little gets through, as a glow. Take one tiny step.

items.f: A neutrino meets the whole Earth
items.b: Goes through. Neutrinos are tiny particles from the Sun. Almost all of them pass right through the Earth. Jump forward.

rules: Mark a start line and a finish line, about 8 big jumps apart. A long hallway or the middle of a room works.
The players stand on the start line. One person is the caller.
The caller reads the front of a card out loud.
Players decide fast. If it would go through, jump forward one big jump. If it would be stopped, freeze where you are.
The caller reads the back. Anyone who moved the wrong way goes back one jump.
The first player to cross the finish line wins, and becomes the next caller.

setup.art: Two children standing on a start line made of a dupatta laid on the floor, and a woman holding a card.
setup.caption: 1. Make a start line and a finish line.

setup.art: One child jumping forward and one child frozen in place, while the caller reads a card.
setup.caption: 2. Hear the card. Jump forward or freeze.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Mark the lines with a dupatta, a rope or tape. 3. Read the rules.
flow.say: When I read a card, think fast. Does it go through, or is it stopped? Jump if it goes through. Freeze if it is stopped.
flow.kid: Stand on the start line. Listen to the card. Jump or freeze.

flow.do: 1. Read the front of each card. 2. Wait for every player to jump or freeze. 3. Read the back. 4. Send wrong movers back one jump.
flow.say: Water meets a glass window! Jump or freeze?
flow.kid: Listen. Does it go through? Jump. Is it stopped? Freeze.
flow.parent: The last card is a surprise. Neutrinos are real, tiny particles that come from the Sun. Nearly all of them pass straight through the whole Earth.

flow.do: 1. At the end, ask the question below.
flow.say: Light and water both met the glass window. Why did one jump and one freeze?
flow.kid: Why did light go through the glass, but water froze?

good: Glass has no holes for water, but light goes through glass itself.

challenges.title: A Rain Window for a Shoebox Room
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. You cut a window in the lid of a shoebox and cover it. It must let light into the box and keep the rain out.
challenges.problem: Make a skylight in the lid of a shoebox. When you peep in through a small hole in the side, the box must be bright inside. When you pour 3 teaspoons of water on the skylight, the paper on the floor of the box must stay dry.
constraints: The window must be at least as big as a matchbox.
Use at most 4 pieces of sticky tape.
materials: a shoebox with a lid, or any cardboard box
a sheet of paper with sketch pen dots, for the floor of the box
clear polythene, foil, cloth, newspaper, a tea strainer or a mosquito net piece
sticky tape and scissors (a grown-up cuts the holes)
a teaspoon, a cup of water and a tray
general: Clear polythene taped over the hole, pulled tight.
A piece of a clear plastic food box, cut by a grown-up and taped over the hole.
creative: A clear polythene roof that slopes, so the water runs off the edge.
A mosquito net piece under the polythene, so the window keeps out both insects and rain.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own skylight. Test it with 3 teaspoons of water, then peep inside. If the dots on the floor run, find where the water got in, and make it better.

setup.art: A shoebox lid with a matchbox-sized hole cut in it, and a small peep hole in the side of the box.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts a window in the lid and a peep hole in the side.

setup.art: A child taping clear polythene over the hole in the lid.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the window.

setup.art: A child pouring a teaspoon of water on the polythene skylight, then peeping in through the side hole.
setup.caption: 3. Pour the water. Peep in. Is it bright? Is the floor dry?

flow.do: 1. Cut a window in the lid, about the size of a matchbox. 2. Cut a peep hole, as big as a coin, in one side. 3. Put the dotted paper on the floor of the box.
flow.say: The window must do two jobs. What are they? Which material will you use? Why?
flow.kid: What two jobs must the window do? Which material will you pick? Why?

flow.do: 1. Your child covers the window with their chosen material. 2. They use at most 4 pieces of tape.
flow.say: Cover the window. Make it tight at the edges, so water cannot creep in there.
flow.kid: Cover the window. Tape the edges tight.

flow.do: 1. Put the box on the tray, next to a window or a lamp. 2. Your child peeps in through the side hole. 3. Pour 3 teaspoons of water on the skylight, one at a time. 4. Wait one minute, then open the lid and check the dots.
flow.say: Peep in first. Is it bright inside? Now pour the water. Wait a minute. Are the dots still sharp?
flow.kid: Peep in. Is it bright? Pour the water. Wait. Are the dots dry?

ask.q: Did your window do both jobs?
good: Yes. It was bright inside and the dots stayed sharp.
No. Water crept in at the tape, so I need to tape the edges better.

flow.do: 1. If the dots ran, find where the water got in. 2. Your child changes one thing and tests again.
flow.say: Where did the water get in? What one thing will you change?
flow.kid: Where did water get in? Change one thing. Test again.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: you can see clearly through it
gets longer when you pull it
items.why: These are four of the property words in this unit.

items.p: In the light and water test, what happened to the teaspoon of water on the clear polythene?
opts: It sat on top, and the tumbler stayed dry
items.why: Polythene has no holes or gaps, so the water could not get through. Picking 'ran into the tumbler' may mean thinking see-through things let water through.
items.context: This question is about the light and water test. You look at a window through five materials, then pour a teaspoon of water on each one over a glass tumbler.

items.p: Sort these into 'lets light through' and 'blocks light'.
items.why: Glass and polythene let light through the material itself. A tea strainer lets it through its holes. Foil, steel and wood are opaque.
items.context: This question is about the light and water test. You look at a window through five materials, then pour a teaspoon of water on each one over a glass tumbler.

items.p: Draw the tumbler with polythene on top, and the tumbler with the tea strainer on top, after you poured the water. Show where the water ended up.
items.a: Water sitting in a little pool on the polythene with a dry tumbler below. Water at the bottom of the tumbler under the strainer.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the water in two different places: on top of the polythene, and inside the tumbler under the strainer.
items.context: This question is about the light and water test. You look at a window through five materials, then pour a teaspoon of water on each one over a glass tumbler.
items.art: Two empty tumbler outlines side by side, labelled polythene and tea strainer.

items.p: If you can see through something, water can always get through it too.
items.why: False. You can see through clear polythene and glass, but water stays out. Light passes through the material itself, and water needs a gap.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did the water go through the tea strainer?
items.a: Because the tea strainer has lots of small holes, and water goes through the holes.
items.why: A strong answer names the holes. Water gets through a material only where there is a gap.

items.p: Three of these keep water out. Which one lets water through?
items.why: A cotton towel is made of fibres with gaps between them, so water soaks in and through. The other three are waterproof.

items.p: Label each picture: transparent, translucent or opaque.
labels: a cotton hanky held up to a window
items.why: Through glass you see a clear picture. A hanky only glows. Steel and foil let no light through.
items.art: Four small pictures with an empty label line under each.

items.p: Kamala, a girl in Class 2, tested 5 materials with water. 2 of them kept the water out. How many let the water through?
items.why: 5 take away 2 leaves 3.
items.context: This question is about the light and water test. You look at a window through five materials, then pour a teaspoon of water on each one over a glass tumbler.

items.p: Selvi and her brother Ravi are choosing a cover for a small window in their flat.

views.says: Use clear polythene. It lets the light in and keeps the rain out.
Use a mosquito net. It lets fresh air in and keeps the mosquitoes out.

items.ask: Whose cover would you choose? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason, such as 'the polythene kept water out in our test'. It also says what the other gets right, such as 'the net lets air in, and polythene does not'.
items.why: Both are right about something. Polythene keeps rain out but blocks air. A net lets air in but also lets rain in. The best choice depends on the weather and the job.

items.p: Anu wants to cover her school book in the rain, and still read its name on the front. Which cover is best?
items.why: Clear polythene is waterproof and transparent, so it does both jobs. Foil is waterproof but opaque. Newspaper lets water through.

items.p: In the pull, not push activity, what happened when you tried to push the toy with the thread?
opts: The thread bent and went floppy, and the toy stayed still
items.why: A thread is strong when pulled, but it bends when pushed. So it cannot push a toy.
items.context: This question is about the pull, not push activity. You tie a cotton thread to a small toy and try to pull it, then push it, across the floor.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why does a rubber band hold a bundle of pencils tighter than a cotton thread?
items.a: The rubber band is stretched round the pencils, and it pulls back to get shorter. When pencils come out, it shrinks and stays tight. The thread cannot shrink, so it goes loose.
items.why: A strong answer says the band is stretchy and springs back. The thread stays the same length.
items.context: This question is about the tight bundle activity. You hold one bundle of pencils with a rubber band and one with a cotton thread, then take some pencils out.

items.p: Design a monsoon suit for a superhero. Label one part that is waterproof, one that is stretchy, one that is strong and one that is see-through.
items.a: For example, a waterproof polythene cape, stretchy rubber cuffs, a strong cotton belt and a see-through plastic face shield.
items.why: A strong design gives each part a property that suits its job, and names a real material for it.
items.art: An empty outline of a superhero figure, with four label lines pointing to the head, body, wrists and waist.

items.p: Anjali and Meera are arguing about whether a rubber band is strong.

views.says: A rubber band is strong. It held our bundle of pencils tight.
A rubber band is not strong. It snaps when you pull it too far.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and sees that both are partly right. A band is strong enough to hold pencils, but it snaps if stretched too far.
items.why: Whether a material is 'strong' depends on the job. The same band is strong for one job and too weak for another.

items.p: Stretchy things are always weak.
items.why: False. Spider silk is very stretchy and also very strong for how thin it is.

items.p: Put these in order, from the one that lets the most light through to the one that lets the least.
items.why: Polythene gives a clear picture. A thin hanky glows brightly. Newspaper glows faintly. Foil lets no light through.
items.context: This question is about the light and water test. You look at a window through five materials, then pour a teaspoon of water on each one over a glass tumbler.

items.p: A material that lets some light through, but no clear picture, is called ____.
items.why: A thin hanky and your closed eyelids are translucent.

items.p: Lakshmi wants a bathroom window that lets light in, but stops people outside from seeing in. Which material should she pick?
items.why: Translucent frosted glass lets light in but shows no clear picture. Clear glass lets people see in. Steel blocks the light.

items.p: Match each job to the property it needs most.
items.why: Each job needs a different property. Spectacles must be see-through, a kite string must not break, a waistband must stretch, and an umbrella must keep rain off.

items.p: Label the parts of an umbrella with the property each part needs.
a: handle: strong, and easy to hold
items.why: The cloth keeps rain off. The ribs hold the cloth out in the wind without bending. The handle must not break.
items.art: An open umbrella with label lines pointing to the cloth, the ribs and the handle.

items.p: In the Four Boxes game, Revathi put 4 cards in each of the 4 boxes. How many cards did she sort?
items.why: 4 boxes with 4 cards each: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16.
items.context: This question is about the Four Boxes game. You sort cards of things into four boxes: see-through or not, and keeps water out or lets it through.

opts: You can see clearly through it
quiz.why: Opaque materials, like foil and wood, let no light through. Picking 'see clearly through it' mixes it up with transparent.
You can see clearly through glass. Steel and wood are opaque.

quiz.p: Nisha, a girl in Mysuru, pours a teaspoon of water on kitchen foil over a tumbler. What happens?
opts: The water drips into the tumbler
quiz.why: Foil has no holes, so it is waterproof. Picking 'soaks it up' mixes foil up with paper or cloth.

quiz.p: You can see through clear polythene. Why does water still stay on top of it?
opts: The polythene has no holes for water, and light goes through the plastic itself
quiz.why: Water needs a gap to get through. Light can pass through the plastic itself. Picking 'too heavy' may mean thinking heavy things cannot pass through holes.

quiz.p: Why does a tea strainer let water through?
opts: It is full of small holes
quiz.why: Water goes through the holes. A steel plate has no holes, and keeps water out.

quiz.p: Which two properties does a window need most?
quiz.why: A window must let light in and keep rain out. Picking 'opaque' would make the room dark.

quiz.p: Farhan, a boy in Kolkata, tries to push a toy car with a thread. What happens?
opts: The thread bends, and the car stays still
quiz.why: A thread is strong when pulled, but it bends when pushed. Picking 'snaps' may mean thinking a thread is weak. It is strong, but only for pulling.

quiz.p: You take 3 pencils out of two bundles. Which bundle stays tight?
opts: The one held by a cotton thread
The one held by a rubber band
quiz.why: The stretched rubber band shrinks back and keeps holding. The thread stays the same length and goes loose.

quiz.p: Which material is best for a mosquito net?
quiz.why: A net lets air through its holes but the holes are too small for mosquitoes. Polythene and foil would block the air.

quiz.p: Before you test a material, what should you do first?
opts: Guess what will happen, and say why
Test it many times without thinking
quiz.why: A guess with a reason helps you notice if the test surprises you.

applications: Windows, spectacles and bottles use glass or clear plastic, because they are transparent and keep water in or out.
Raincoats, umbrellas and school bag covers are made of waterproof materials.
Tea strainers, sieves and mosquito nets have holes on purpose, to let some things through and keep others back.
Hair bands, waistbands and the bands fruit sellers use are stretchy, so they hold things tight.
Ropes, kite strings and fibres like Kevlar are strong when pulled, so they are used to pull, lift and hold.

open_questions.q: Can people make a coating that keeps water off as well as a lotus leaf, and lasts for years?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have copied the tiny waxy bumps on lotus and chembu leaves. But the copies usually wear off when they are rubbed. Making one that lasts is still being worked on.
In some tests light acts like a wave. In others it acts like tiny packets of energy. Scientists can work out exactly what light will do, but what it really is underneath is still argued about.

What stretchy things are you wearing today?
If you made a window for a doll's house, what would you use? Why?

maths.problem: Megha, a girl in Pune, did the light and water test with 5 materials. Water stayed on top of 2 of them. Draw a block for each material in two columns: 'kept water out' and 'let water through'. Which column is taller, and by how many blocks?
maths.answer: 'Let water through' is taller, by 1 block.
maths.explain: 5 materials take away the 2 that kept water out leaves 3 that let it through. 3 blocks is 1 more than 2 blocks.
maths.context: This question is about the light and water test. You look at a window through five materials, then pour a teaspoon of water on each one over a glass tumbler.
maths.why_maths: Blocks in two columns show at a glance which result was more common.

maths.problem: Draw two circles that overlap. Label one 'lets light through' and the other 'keeps water out'. Where do these go: clear polythene, a tea strainer, kitchen foil and newspaper?
maths.answer: Polythene goes in the middle, in both circles. The strainer goes only in 'lets light through'. Foil goes only in 'keeps water out'. Newspaper goes outside both circles.
maths.explain: Polythene does both things, so it belongs in the overlap. The strainer lets light through but not water out. Foil keeps water out but blocks light. Newspaper lets only a faint glow through, which is not a clear picture, and it lets water through.
maths.context: This question is about the light and water test. You look at a window through five materials, then pour a teaspoon of water on each one over a glass tumbler.
maths.why_maths: Overlapping circles show which materials have both properties at once.

maths.problem: You made a bundle of 10 pencils with a rubber band and took 3 out. How many pencils were left in the bundle? The thread bundle also had the same number left, but it fell apart. Why did the same number of pencils give two different results?
maths.answer: 7 pencils were left. The rubber band shrank to hold 7 tightly. The thread stayed the size it was for 10, so it was too loose for 7.
maths.explain: 10 take away 3 is 7. The number of pencils was the same, so the difference came from the materials: one can get shorter, and one cannot.
maths.context: This question is about the tight bundle activity. You hold one bundle of pencils with a rubber band and one with a cotton thread, then take some pencils out.
maths.why_maths: Taking away tells us how many pencils were left. Comparing two bundles with the same number shows the material made the difference.

maths.problem: The Four Boxes game has 4 boxes and 4 cards in each box. Then you add a card for 'a glass bangle'. How many cards are there now, and which box does the new card go in?
maths.answer: 17 cards. The bangle goes in Box 1, see-through and keeps water out.
maths.explain: 4 groups of 4 make 16. One more makes 17. Glass is transparent and has no holes, so water stays out.
maths.context: This question is about the Four Boxes game. You sort cards of things into four boxes: see-through or not, and keeps water out or lets it through.
maths.why_maths: Counting equal groups tells us how many cards there are without counting each one.

roots.context: We have tested what gets through polythene, foil, cloth, newspaper and a tea strainer. Now we ask what that tells us about materials, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Water sat on the clear polythene and never dripped into the tumbler, so it has no holes. Yet you saw the window clearly through it. Light passed through the solid plastic, where water could not. What gets through a material depends on what is trying to get through.
deep_truth.habit: We think of things as either open or closed, like a door. We expect anything that lets something through to have holes. The test showed one sheet of plastic open to light and closed to water.
deep_truth.evidence: In the light and water test, you saw the window clearly through the polythene. A teaspoon of water sat on it for a full minute, and the tumbler stayed dry. The tea strainer let both through, because it has holes.

three.who_am_i: Your eyelids are translucent: shut them in a bright room and you see a glow. Your skin keeps most water out when you bathe.
three.what_is_life: A chembu leaf grows a waxy skin that rain rolls off. Living beings grow the materials they need.
three.what_is_this_world: Sunlight passes through the air and a window to reach you, while the roof stops the rain. Each material lets some things in and keeps others out.

roots.thread: Polythene, foil, cotton and steel are all made of tiny particles holding on to each other. How the particles are packed decides what can pass. Water needs a gap, and polythene has none. Light needs no gap, and passes through the plastic itself. Everything is conscious, down to these tiny particles, and each material meets light and water in its own way.

teachings.teaching: We cut doors and windows to make a room. It is the empty space in them that makes the room useful.
teachings.link: A tea strainer is useful because of its holes. A window is useful because it lets light in. The Tao Te Ching, from China, asks us to notice what the openings do.

teachings.teaching: The face of truth is covered by a golden lid. Open it, so that I may see what is true.
teachings.link: A shiny golden lid is beautiful, but it is opaque, so it hides what is under it. To see, we need a material that lets light through, or we must lift the lid.

science.text: Glass and clear plastic have no holes that water can pass through. Light gets through because their particles let most light pass without soaking it up.
Light acts like a wave in some tests and like tiny packets of energy in others. What light really is underneath is still argued about.

other_view.view: They say a sheet of plastic has no awareness at all. They explain everything it does with particles and forces, and they find no need for a mind to explain it.

practice.title: Light through your eyelids
practice.say: Sit facing a bright window. Close your eyes gently. Is it fully dark? Notice the soft glow. That is light coming through your eyelids. Now cover your closed eyes with your palms. Notice how much darker it is. Take three slow breaths. Then take your hands away, and feel the glow come back.
practice.kid: Sit facing a bright window. Close your eyes. Can you see a glow? Cover your eyes with your hands. Is it darker? Breathe slowly three times. Take your hands away.

ask: The polythene let light in but kept water out. Was it open or closed?
When your eyes are shut and you see a glow, are you seeing?
Is there anything that nothing at all can pass through?
roots.art: A child sitting with eyes closed facing a bright window covered with clear plastic, with rain running down the outside and soft light falling on the child's face.

Cambridge Primary Science Stage 2, Unit 3 'Getting materials right': the property words (waterproof, flexible, strong, transparent) and one material having many properties. The tests here are new, so as not to repeat the testing materials unit at the same level.
science: Water passes through porous materials (paper, cotton) through the gaps between fibres; polyethylene film and aluminium foil are non-porous.

Transparency of glass and clear polymers: visible light is not absorbed by their electrons and is little scattered, because the material is uniform with no internal boundaries (any optics or materials textbook).

C. V. Raman, 'On the molecular scattering of light in water and the colour of the sea', Proceedings of the Royal Society A 101 (1922), 64-80, written after his 1921 sea voyage. Lord Rayleigh had said the deep blue of the sea is the sky seen by reflection.

Stephanie Kwolek at DuPont, 1965: a cloudy, low-viscosity solution of a para-aramid polymer, spun after persuading Charles Smullen, gave the fibre later sold as Kevlar (Science History Institute; Kwolek's own accounts).
Kevlar's strength-to-weight is about five times that of steel (DuPont); breaking elongation only a few percent.
Spider dragline silk combines high strength with high extensibility (Gosline and others, Journal of Experimental Biology, 1999).
E. D. Zanotto, 'Do cathedral glasses flow?', American Journal of Physics 66 (1998), 392-395: room-temperature flow of glass would take far longer than the age of the Universe.
Neutrinos from the Sun pass through the Earth almost without interacting (any particle physics textbook).

W. Barthlott and C. Neinhuis, 'Purity of the sacred lotus, or escape from contamination in biological surfaces', Planta 202 (1997), 1-8: the lotus effect. Durable artificial superhydrophobic coatings remain a research problem.
sources.walkthrough: Every step was thought through for a city flat. A teaspoon is about 5 ml. On polythene or foil held over a tumbler with a rubber band, it sits as a small pool, and the tumbler stays dry. On thin cotton it drips through within a few seconds. On a single layer of newspaper it soaks in, and the underside is wet within a minute, with a few drops sometimes falling. In a tea strainer it runs straight through. Held close to the eye in front of a daylit window, clear polythene gives a clear view, the strainer gives a dim view through its mesh, thin cotton glows, newspaper glows faintly and foil is dark. The spine is the intro, the yes-or-no grid and the light and water test (session 1, about 37 minutes), then the explanations, Roots and the quiz (session 2, about 30 minutes).

playtest: Thought through as a parent and child in a flat: the yes-or-no grid, the light and water test, pull not push, the tight bundle, both games and the shoebox skylight, with minutes, materials and steps checked. The tests are new for this level: the testing materials unit already has a stretch test, a waterproof spot test and a bottle lift, and the Class 3 units have layered materials and oil spots, so this unit asks whether light and water get through the same materials.
